zone: Olympic interior — the Quinault head, LaCrosse Basin and the last North Fork summits
_areas_note: THREE of the seven peaks handed to me were removed, and two of them were not summits at all. STEEPLE ROCK is a roadside crag: a 200 ft basalt spire about two miles down the Obstruction Point road from the Hurricane Ridge visitor centre, holding five short routes and some scrambling, most of them under half an hour. You park, you climb it, you drive home. There is no approach, no camp and nothing for a camping zone to say. THE FULL MONTEY is the same class of thing on the other side of the range — it is one of the Tyler Peak crags on the pillow basalt above the upper Dungeness road, reached by driving the 2860 road to a numbered spur and then walking up to the upper bench from the base of a neighbouring wall. Also a crag, also no camp. Neither belongs in this file and neither needs a zone at all; if the catalog wants a camping section for them the honest answer is that the nearest legal overnight ground is the Forest Service campgrounds low on the Dungeness road, which is a car-camping fact rather than an approach. MOUNT TOM is a real summit and is genuinely excluded for the opposite reason: it stands on the west end of the Olympus massif and every party reaches it exactly the way they reach Olympus — eighteen miles up the Hoh, Glacier Meadows, the moraine, and then a traverse west below the Olympus summits from the Snow Dome. Those camps are already written up, in full, in the Mount Olympus file. Writing them again here would put two answers on screen for one question, so the id is left out and belongs on that file's areas list instead. ONE PEAK WAS MISFILED RATHER THAN REMOVED. CHIMNEY PEAK is not a Skokomish objective. It stands immediately north above Enchanted Valley, its southeast face rising some 4,800 ft out of the valley floor in under a mile, and the approach leaves the East Fork Quinault trail at about the nine-mile mark. Nothing about it touches the North Fork Skokomish, First Divide or Home Sweet Home. It is kept here because the East Fork Quinault serves it and because the same trail system reaches LaCrosse Basin, but a party sent to Staircase for it will be on the wrong side of the range. WHAT IS NOT REPEATED: the Enchanted Valley chalet camp and Anderson Pass, the Graves Creek campground and the whole upper Elwha chain including Chicago Camp and Low Divide are all covered properly in the Elwha and Enchanted Valley file, and Marmot Lake, Camp Pleasant, Nine Stream and Home Sweet Home are covered in the Staircase file. None of them appears below. Note also that the Staircase side of this country has been under a fire closure since 2025 and much of it was still shut in mid-2026, which is part of why the Dosewallips and Quinault approaches described here matter more than they used to.

sites.name: Sixteen Mile Camp — the base directly under Mount Lawson
sites.capacity: Four established sites on the river flat, and it is rarely contested — almost everyone walking this valley is bound for Low Divide and passes straight through
sites.water: Reliable. The North Fork Quinault runs at the camp, which is also the reason the camp exists and the reason it can be unreachable; treat everything.
sites.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The North Fork Quinault is not a quota area, so this is one of the easier permits in the park, but nothing here is held back as a same-day walk-up and camps this far in do not always surface in an online search — telephone the wilderness information centre if it will not show. An approved animal-resistant food container is mandatory throughout the park wilderness and free loaners are handed out with permits. This camp sits below the 3,500 ft fire line, so fires are legal in the established rings when no seasonal ban is running, and bans are usual by midsummer.
sites.notes: This is the camp for MOUNT LAWSON and effectively the only one. The peak rises about 3,800 ft above the river in a mile and a third, straight out of the drainage the camp sits in, and the climb is a class 2 slog on steep forest and open slope rather than anything technical — the work is the approach, not the summit. The camp is roughly twelve miles up the valley from the North Fork trailhead, past Wolf Bar, Halfway House, Elip Creek and Trapper Shelter, and the walk is gentle until the last few miles where the valley narrows and the trail climbs and drops across steep sidehill. THE FORDS ARE THE WHOLE PLANNING PROBLEM. There are three of them — Wild Rose Creek, Elip Creek and the North Fork itself right at this camp — and the river crossing here is regularly impassable during snowmelt or after heavy rain. Parties have been turned around at it having walked twelve miles. Go in late summer when the river is low, carry poles, and treat a high river as a trip-ending condition rather than something to force. Reach the trailhead by the North Shore Road; the South Shore Road has been washed out and a phone will still try to send you that way.

sites.name: Elip Creek and the lower North Fork Quinault camps
sites.capacity: Elip Creek has four sites, Wolf Bar five and Halfway House two. Trapper Shelter above them holds two small spots and is best treated as day or emergency use only rather than a planned night.
sites.water: Reliable at all of them — the river or the named side creek. The lower valley is rainforest and water is never the constraint here.
sites.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance; not a quota area and usually obtainable at short notice. Animal-resistant food container mandatory. All of these sit well below the fire line so established rings are legal outside a burn ban.
sites.notes: These break the walk to Sixteen Mile rather than serving any summit directly, and that matters more than it sounds: the drive to the North Fork trailhead is long, most parties arrive in the afternoon, and twelve miles with a climbing pack on the same day is an unpleasant way to start. Wolf Bar at about two and a half miles is the late-arrival camp, Elip Creek at roughly six and a half is the natural halfway stop, and Trapper Shelter a mile and a half further is the last of them before the valley steepens. Grades are easy to Trapper and then the trail begins working up and down high above the river. Two of the three fords are below Sixteen Mile, so a night here also lets you look at the water level before committing to the upper valley. Deep old-growth forest, heavy shade, mosquitoes in early summer and no views whatsoever — this is shelter and mileage, nothing more.

sites.name: Pyrites Creek — where the Chimney Peak approach leaves the trail
sites.capacity: A modest forested riverside camp with a handful of sites, quieter than the valley above it because most parties push the extra four miles to the chalet meadow
sites.water: Reliable — the East Fork Quinault and the creek the camp is named for both run all season
sites.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and THE EAST FORK QUINAULT IS A QUOTA AREA. It has been run under a nightly cap of thirty permits or roughly two hundred people since 2024, so this is a booking to make the day reservations open rather than a fortnight out. The summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and releases in one drop in mid-April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over plus a six dollar booking fee, or an annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY REQUIRED IN THIS VALLEY and enforced rather than advised — the Enchanted Valley was closed over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Free loaners at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness offices.
sites.notes: This is the camp for CHIMNEY PEAK, and the reason it rather than the chalet meadow is that the approach leaves the East Fork Quinault trail at about nine miles, which is where this camp sits. Push on to the chalet and you have walked four miles past your own turning and given yourself them back again in the morning. The peak stands immediately north above the valley with its southeast face rising something like 4,800 ft in less than a mile, streaming waterfalls into the valley below — spectacular from the trail and completely useless as a line of ascent. The climb goes round to the southwest ridge and is class 3 scrambling once you are on it, with the first ascent not made until 1941, which says something about how the ground below it behaves. Expect a long, steep, largely trackless day out of the valley floor. June through September is the workable window. The walk in from Graves Creek is thirteen miles to the chalet with staged camps at Pony Bridge and O'Neil Creek before this one, so most parties take two easy days in rather than one hard one.

sites.name: Lake LaCrosse and Hart Lake — the base for Mount La Crosse and White Mountain
sites.capacity: A small number of sites spread between the two lakes, in and above open subalpine basin. Neither holds a crowd and the meadow ground is fragile, so use the established pads rather than making new ones.
sites.water: Reliable — both lakes hold through the season and the outlet creeks run into autumn. This is the last dependable water before anything you climb from here; the slopes and the unnamed glacier between the two summits carry no running source once the snow has gone.
sites.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. This basin is not itself one of the named quota areas, but the East Fork Quinault approach to it is, so which trailhead you walk in from changes what you have to book — check the whole itinerary rather than just the camp. An animal-resistant food container is required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the parkwide 3,500 ft line. Elk work this basin heavily and bears are regular visitors.
sites.notes: THE camp for both MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN, which stand less than a mile apart on either side of a small unnamed glacier directly above the basin. Both are scrambles rather than climbs — La Crosse at 6,417 ft goes at class 2 and was first climbed in 1928, White Mountain at 6,378 ft is class 2 as well — so from a camp here the two together are a single long day rather than an expedition. Lake LaCrosse sits at about 4,800 ft, roughly 400 ft higher and a mile and a half further than Marmot Lake, with Hart Lake in between; Marmot is covered in the Staircase file and is a perfectly good camp, but it is further from these two summits and it is the wrong side of the shelf. THE APPROACH IS THE ENTIRE DIFFICULTY AND THERE ARE THREE OF THEM, none short. From the Dosewallips you go up the West Fork and over LaCrosse Pass. From the East Fork Quinault you go through Enchanted Valley and over Anderson Pass. From the Duckabush you come up the river and over O'Neil Pass. Every one of those is two days in for most parties carrying gear, which is why these summits see so little traffic. July through September; the basin holds snow late and the passes either side of it later still.

sites.name: O'Neil Pass and the upper Duckabush shelf
sites.capacity: Informal rather than developed — a small amount of workable ground on the shelf near the pass, room for a party or two, with no facilities of any kind
sites.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal runnels only, and the pass itself dries out as the summer goes on. Fill at Lake LaCrosse or down in the basin before coming up; this is ground you carry water to.
sites.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. Which booking you need depends on the approach — the Duckabush side is not a quota area, the East Fork Quinault is. Animal-resistant food container mandatory. No fires at this elevation. If the ground you intend to use is not an established site, say so when you book and expect to be routed to a cross-country zone permit arranged by telephone rather than online.
sites.notes: A high, exposed alternative to the lake basin for a party that wants to be moving early on WHITE MOUNTAIN or that is traversing rather than going in and back. The pass sits at roughly 4,900 ft on the long shelf that carries the trail in a slow horseshoe between the Duckabush head and the East Fork Quinault, and Chimney Peak and the Anderson massif are both in view from it — which is the honest reason most people stop here rather than any advantage on climbing day. The trade is bad: it saves very little on either summit and it costs you shelter, water and any chance of a comfortable night. There is nothing to hide behind and the weather arrives off the Quinault with no warning. Treat it as a tactical stop on a longer route rather than a base. Snow lies on the north side of the shelf into midsummer and the meadow ground either side of the trail is soft enough to hold a footprint for years, so stay on rock or bare tread.

sites.name: Honeymoon Meadows and Camp Siberia — the West Fork Dosewallips side of LaCrosse Pass
sites.capacity: Honeymoon Meadows is an open riverside meadow camp with several sites and is the pleasant one; Camp Siberia near Anderson Pass is smaller, higher and colder, with a few spots and an old shelter frame. Diamond Meadow and Big Timber lower down break the walk further.
sites.water: Reliable at all of them — the West Fork Dosewallips runs beside the trail the whole way and the meadows carry side streams into the autumn
sites.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The Dosewallips side is not a quota area and these camps are usually available at short notice, which is a real advantage over the Quinault approach to the same country. Animal-resistant food container required. Honeymoon Meadows sits near the fire line and Camp Siberia above it, so assume no fires at either.
sites.notes: This is the eastern way to LaCrosse Basin and the one to use when the East Fork Quinault quota is gone. From the road end the trail runs up to Dose Forks at about 7.6 miles, Big Timber at 10.3, Diamond Meadow at 12.7 and Honeymoon Meadows at 15, with the LaCrosse Pass trail branching a little before that and Camp Siberia at around 16 near Anderson Pass. From Honeymoon Meadows the pass trail climbs roughly 2,000 ft in a couple of miles, the first 1,500 in forest before it breaks into open meadow, and drops the other side toward the LaCrosse Basin lakes — so MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN are two days in from here rather than one. THE ROAD IS THE CATCH AND IT HAS BEEN FOR TWO DECADES. The Dosewallips road washed out well below the old trailhead and has never been rebuilt, so the walk starts with several miles of abandoned road before any trail begins, and every mileage quoted above is measured from the old road end rather than from where you will actually park. Bicycles help on that stretch. Add the road walk to every figure before deciding this is the short way.
